questions.explanation: mission-critical communications: Any communications where disruption will result in the failure of the mission at hand.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: Any communications where disruption will result in the failure of the mission at hand.

questions.explanation: Mission-critical communications are any communications where disruption will result in failure of the mission at hand. An interoperable system links different agencies together; simplex is one-direction-at-a-time radio; paging sends alerts - none of those describe what happens if the link is lost.
questions.question: A dispatcher warns crews to keep one link clear during a building collapse rescue: if that link goes down or gets tied up, the rescue effort itself will fail. Communications with that much riding on them are called:

questions.explanation: channel: An assigned frequency or frequencies that are used to carry voice and/or data communications.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: An assigned frequency or frequencies that are used to carry voice and/or data communications.

questions.explanation: A channel is an assigned frequency or frequencies used to carry voice and/or data communications. A band is a whole range of frequencies, such as 30-300 MHz; a repeater rebroadcasts a signal on a second frequency; a base station is the fixed radio hardware at headquarters.
questions.question: At a working fire, dispatch moves your crew off the main frequency: "All units switch to TAC 3 and stay there for this incident." TAC 3, the assigned frequency your crew now talks on, is an example of a:

questions.explanation: repeater: A special base station radio that receives messages and signals on one frequency and then automatically retransmits them on a second frequency.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: A special base station radio that receives messages and signals on one frequency and then automatically retransmits them on a second frequency.

questions.explanation: A repeater is a special base station radio that receives messages on one frequency and automatically retransmits them on a second frequency, extending their range. A base station is the fixed transmitter and receiver at headquarters; a scanner only receives; a cellular telephone works through cell sites.
questions.question: Your portable radio's signal is too weak to reach dispatch from inside a concrete building, but your message gets through anyway: a hilltop unit picks it up and rebroadcasts it, stronger, on a second frequency. That hilltop unit is a:

questions.explanation: mental model: The picture an individual has in his or her head of “what’s going on” in a given situation.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: The picture an individual has in his or her head of “what’s going on” in a given situation.

questions.explanation: Your mental model is the picture in your head of what is going on in a given situation; when it is wrong, you have to rebuild it from what you actually find. The chief concern is the most urgent problem your assessment identifies - here, the possible heart problem, not the fall.
questions.question: Dispatch describes a "minor fall," so you walk in picturing a quick lift assist. Instead you find the patient pale, sweating, and clutching his chest - and for a moment you keep treating it as a fall call. The picture in your head that you walked in with is your:

questions.explanation: cultural imposition: When one person imposes his or her beliefs, values, and practices on another because he or she believes his or her ideals are superior.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: When one person imposes his or her beliefs, values, and practices on another because he or she believes his or her ideals are superior.

questions.explanation: Cultural imposition is imposing your own beliefs, values, and practices on another person because you believe your ideals are superior. Ethnocentrism is the attitude of judging your culture superior; imposition is the act of forcing your practices on the patient.
questions.question: A patient declines a treatment step for religious reasons. Your partner insists anyway, telling the family, "We do it our way - it's better," and pushes his own practices on them over their objections. Your partner is guilty of:

questions.explanation: MED channels: VHF and UHF channels that the Federal Communications Commission has designated exclusively for EMS use.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: VHF and UHF channels that the Federal Communications Commission has designated exclusively for EMS use.

questions.explanation: The MED channels are the VHF and UHF channels the Federal Communications Commission designated exclusively for EMS use. A trunked talk group is assigned from a shared pool of frequencies, simplex is a one-direction-at-a-time mode, and paging channels carry alerts - none of those are reserved for EMS.
questions.question: You need to call in a report to the hospital, and the regular traffic channels are jammed with fire and police calls. You switch to the set of VHF and UHF frequencies the federal regulators set aside for EMS use only. You are now transmitting on:
